subject: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals
parts:
Hi,

Inspired by the example of modeling a mixture of normals in stan (sec 9.2) I thought using the similar approach to multivariate normals.  My question - is the code below correct or should I put increment_log_prob of multinormal_log inside for loop?

Thanks for any advice,
Linas

parameters {
  real <lower = 0, upper  = 1> theta; // mixing proportions
  matrix a_mu [N]];
  matrix [N, N] a_Sigma;
  matrix b_mu [N]];
  matrix [N, N] b_Sigma;
}
model {
  real ps[2]; // temp for log component densities
  a_mu ~ normal(0,10);
  b_mu ~ normal(0,10);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    ps[1] <- log(theta);
    ps[2] <- log1m(theta);
    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(ps));
   }
   increment_log_prob (multi_normal_log (y, a_mu, a_Sigma));
   increment_log_prob (multi_normal_log (y, b_mu, b_Sigma));
}

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals
parts:
For every observation i, you need to do log_sum_exp(ps[1] + multi_normal_log (y[i], a_mu, a_Sigma), ps[2] + multi_normal_log (y[i], b_mu, b_Sigma)). That is the entire likelihood for the data y.

You might want to tighten those priors for a_mu and b_mu, unless you believe this to appropriately reflect the scale of your expectation. Also, your variance-covariance matrices still need to be properly constrained.

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals
parts:
You need to distinguish the number of observations N from the dimension D of each observation. You also misspecified the mean vectors as matrices.

data {
  int<lower=1> N;  // number of independent observations
  int<lower=2> D;  // dimension of each independent observation
  vector[D] y[N];  // array of vectors of observations
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> theta; // mixing proportions
  vector[D] a_mu;
  matrix[D, D] a_Sigma;
  vector[D] b_mu;
  matrix [D, D] b_Sigma;

}
model {
  real ps[2];  // temp for log component densities

ps[1] <- log(theta);
  ps[2] <- log1m(theta);

a_mu ~ normal(0,10);
  b_mu ~ normal(0,10);

  for (n in 1:N)

log_sum_exp(ps[1] + multi_normal_log (y[i], a_mu, a_Sigma), ps[2] + multi_normal_log (y[i], b_mu, b_Sigma)).
}

Note that the model is currently unidentifiable as label switching of a_mu and b_mu is possible. To resolve this in the bivariate case, specify a separate parameter (i.e. ordered vector) for the first elements of a_mu and b_mu, and another parameter for the second elements (an ordinary vector), and then reassemble the elementsnback into a_mu and b_mu in the transformed parameters block (or the model block).

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals
parts:
The following line your code (in the loop) does not make sense as it will always evaluate to zero: increment_log_prob (log_sum_exp (log (theta), log1m (theta))). The sum of the exponents is always one (and the log of that will be zero)! For every data point, you have to do: increment_log_prob (log_sum_exp (log (theta) + LP(y[i] | a_mu*, a_Sigma*), log1m (theta) + LP(y[i] | b_mu*, b_Sigma*) )). The parameters with asterisks represent the conditional distribution of y[i], given parameter a_mu, b_mu, a_Sigma, b_Sigma, and y[-i] (all data but y[i]). NB, these are not the full vector and matrix parameters that you define in the parameter block. See wikipedia on multivariate normal distributions, section conditional distribution of how to calculate that.

It's gonna be very ugly, I guarantee. I would strongly advise you try to find a simpler way to do this. You might want to consider fractional polynomials, or if you know the shape of the association between y and whatever the distance covariate is (I don't see it in your model), you could use a functional association (e.g. a general logistic function or whatnot).

I don't see why you would need theta to "have a sigmoid function", as theta simply represents a mixture weight. IMHO, theta seems fine as it is.

messages.author: 3f22b207863d2049
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals
parts:
Just realized that there's extra ugliness:

You don't know what Gaussian process each y belongs to, so when you calculate a_mu*, a_Sigma* <- f(a_mu, a_Sigma, y[=-i]) , you'd have to marginalize over every possible assignment of y[-i] to GP_a. In short: horrible. You really want to look for something else.

messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: modeling of mixtures of multivariate normals
parts: Although this is an ugly way several folks on this list and outside the list suggested that mixture of Gaussian Processes (GP) might be a solution.  Basically this is calibration of computer simulation data with experimental data.  Green dots indicate experimental data, blue line indicate computer simulation.  Red line is what I have arrived to using Gibbs kernel.  Since of the sudden increase of response (Cp) at input (arclength) close to 0.5 the experimental and computer simulation data don't match each another.  Physically it makes complete sense since those correspond to different flows.  Thus the idea is to represent each flow as two separate GPs with separate set of hyper-parameters.   By assigning different priors on hyper-parameters for each GP one can manipulate smoothness etc.  For example in the chart below GP on the right side is not smooth enough.  Sigmoid was suggested as a way to ensure that those GPs don't interact two much when considered as a mixture.  For this example I am thinking that I could use one GP on the right and normal distribution on the left which I assume will remove identifiability problem.
